name: Marshall Kirk McKusick
bio: spent much of his early career at UC Berkeley’s Computer Systems Research Group. Built the BSD Fast File System, worked on FreeBSD, and has long supported open source.
transcript: I mean, I don't know what you will tell, but some things. So I read like a lot of, I mean, I had a long paper, like where I read a lot of things and your time, like in Berkeley, and I would be interested in like this starting time.

How was it in this time? Like, how do people felt about this time? Did they predict it already, the future and everything that comes? Or was it more like just you worked on cool things and couldn't really imagine the way how it came out like now and like in the late nineties? I think the latter is more correct. I mean, we were a bunch of people and we were really excited about, you know, what we were able to do, but we really had no expectation that it would turn into what it did turn into. And we, along with many other people, we're trying to figure out how to get computers to talk to each other and lots of different ideas were out there. And, you know, in the end, it was the internet stuff that we wrote and, you know, the electronic mail interaction that my husband wrote that, you know, took over the world. I mean, I remember like in 1993, looking up and seeing a billboard with a URL on it. And it's like, holy crap, what's going on here?

But you came like around 1976 to UC Berkeley, right? UC Berkeley, I matriculated in 1976, yes. Was there before already an interesting story that led you then to your work at Berkeley? Because I mean, you spent so much time then as researcher in Berkeley, but was there a pre-preparation or something that led you to this time? Well, the year before I got there in 1975, I'm pretty sure it was, the Unix itself from Bell Labs was just starting to be available. At that point, it was a thing called version five, soon converted to version six. And it ran on a PDP-11, which was a 16-bit machine, not a 32-bit machine. So in 16 bits, you can only have 65 or 64 kilobytes of program and 64 kilobytes of data. And that's about 10,000 lines of C code. So you couldn't write anything that was more than 10,000 lines of C code because it wouldn't fit on the machine. And so they had done a complete operating system, which up to that point, everyone believed you had to do an assembly language, but they had come up with this C, which was really sort of a fancy assembler. I mean, C statements mapped almost one for one to the hardware that it was running on, the PDP-11. And so in 10,000 lines of code, they had the Unix kernel running. Just to give you an idea, a modern device driver today is often as much as 30,000 lines of code just for like a disk device driver. And here they had an entire operating system in 10,000 lines of code. Anyway, so originally that was just at Bell Labs, but they were beginning to make it available to universities and a professor named Professor Robert Fabry
had gone to hear the talk, I think they gave in 73

and was excited. And so they managed to get a PDP-11 and Unix running on it. And it was a bigger machine than the one they had at Bell Labs. It had two disks on it instead of just one. And although the code in theory could work with two disks, at practice, it didn't really work, it would hang. And so they arranged to have Ken Thompson, who was one of the original authors of Unix, log into the console of our PDP-11 in California to debug the disk device driver. And he could do that because of course he worked for the phone company, so paying the long distance rates to dial in for a couple hours, which would have been in the hundreds of dollars of phone time, but it was the phone company, so it didn't matter. Anyway, that worked out well enough that it was up and running. And so by the time I got there, that was the system they had. And that was light years ahead of the punch card system that I'd been using in undergrad at Cornell. And so the fact that I could sit at a terminal and actually work directly with the computer instead of having to punch cards and you run them and wait hours and then get a printed output, et cetera, was just mind boggling. So I was sold instantly on this system. It turned out that Ken Thompson was an alumni of, I mean, he got his degree at Berkeley. And so he actually came out and did a six month sabbatical. And during the time he was doing that sabbatical, he actually did a seminar where he read through the source code of Unix and lectured to people. And Eric Ullman, my husband, actually took that course from him and has his notes and all that, which we actually provided to the Computer History Museum as a memento for them to add to their collection of interesting things. There was a recording done, only an audio recording, but we also have the audio recording of at least of some of the lectures that he did. So when you came to Berkeley, from my understanding, there was already BSD, like people working on BSD, right? And you sort of developed it then in the version that came then to known or what was already developed from the Unix? History there is that my advisor was also the advisor for Bill Joy. So both of us were working on programming language. She was programming language. So we were both doing our PhDs on programming language related topics. And Bill had started creating some utilities to add to what was already on the PDP-11. So the first thing was a Pascal compiler because Pascal was the big hot new language of the time. And so there was a Pascal compiler that had the concept of error correction. So it used to be that as soon as the compiler would hit an error, it would just throw up its hands and give up. And so you had to fix things kind of one at a time. And the goal of what Bill was doing was that the compiler could recover and make sort of some kind of a correction and then continue going. So we could at least get all the way through what you've written and give you several errors to work on. And then of course, the PDP-11 was not very powerful

and heavily overloaded. I mean, 10 or 20 people all trying to use it at once for a fraction of a MIP machine. And so compiling was just too expensive. So instead it just compiled to an intermediate code and then an interpreter ran that code. And that meant that it was about a 10th the amount of time it would have taken to compile it. And it allowed a lot more people to be using the compiler at the same time. So anyhow, Bill also had written some...

On an editor, which eventually turned into VI and EX or NVI today. And so he put together a package which was the Pascal compiler stuff plus this editor plus some other utilities that he'd written and distributed that as the Berkeley software distribution BSD. And that first one was just a set of utilities that you added on top of an existing Unix system. And I don't know, rock bands, when they put out their first album, the name of the album is the name of the group. And then they put out their second album and then what did they do? And it was the same thing with BSD. It was just the Berkeley software distribution. And of course, two years later, he wanted to do an update to it. So what are we gonna call that? And so that became 2BSD and then 3BSD, et cetera. So anyway, Bill and I and Susan Graham's other three students all shared an office. And in those days, we had a phone in our office, landline thing, and the phone would ring and it sat on my desk for whatever reason, but I would just pick it up and just hand it to Bill because it was always somebody calling Bill. I wouldn't even answer it.

And so Bill was totally in charge of these distributions. I mean, they'd call up and they'd say, oh yeah, blah, blah, blah. And Bill would say, well, send me a tape. And they'd write it onto the tape and mail it back to them. Or after a while, I think he just bought a box of tape so he could just mail them to people. Anyway, I mean, there was no licensing, no anything. It just, you put it on a tape and mail it to people. Was it then for free also at this time?

Was it when Bill sent it to them, was it already free or did people take it? That was free. I mean, it was just stuff that he'd written, or a bunch of us had actually written, because I worked a lot on that compiler as well, and other utilities that other people had written. There was a big group, not a big group, but there may be 10 of us that were working on various and sundry things. So that first tape was mostly stuff that Bill had done, but by the second one, it was already a lot of stuff from other people around Berkeley. And people were just writing code and putting it on there and sending it out, and then you get bug reports back, and you'd fix things up, et cetera, et cetera. So Bill got called, or you said there was a call and you gave it to Bill? Bug reports? No, you said there came a call in and you gave it to Bill, and it seemed like there was a story that you couldn't finish. Oh, well, yes, there's more of that story when we start getting to licensing issues, but I'll get to that. Anyway, the upshot of all this was that Bill was getting more and more involved, and other people were starting to get involved, but in particular, there was a desire to have email that was not just around Berkeley, but that you could send to other people. And in those days, the networking was a thing called UUCP, Unix to Unix copy, and it was the... You'd call up the modem on these other people's machine and send stuff across to them, and it was just for copying files, but of course, it would be nice to be able to use that for mail. And so, Eric, who was on a different project doing database-related stuff, but they had a machine that was connected to the ARPANET, and then we also had modems there that could dial out, and so everyone in the... All the professors in the department were banging on his door saying, oh, I want an account on your machine so that I can send email, and he realized, well, if it was possible to just have them send email and have it go out, then they didn't need to have accounts on his machine. They just really wanted the account to do email. So he did a thing called delivermail, which worked between the internal networking at Berkeley, which was this Berknet thing, which was written by this other gentleman named Eric Schmidt, whose name you may recognize because he eventually became the CEO of Google. Anyway, he had written what I can only describe as a rather crappy networking, but it kind of worked to get stuff around the machines at Berkeley, including to the one that Eric ran, and then from there, delivermail would haul it off over either the ARPANET or through the UUCP networking to other places. Of course, UUCP required dialing up, and if it was a long-distance call, that could get expensive because these were slow modems, 1,200 baud initially. So it took a long time to get stuff across. And so this whole UUCP network sprouted up, and there were sort of some backbone nodes. So there was a digital equipment corporation that had a big machine whose sole purpose was to do UUCP, and they had a $20,000-a-month phone bill because of all the calls they made to connect these things up. So thanks to them, we had, you know, email that got around not only to the relatively small number of people on the Internet, but also to the wider universities that were just connected by these phone networks. So anyhow, that proceeded along. So that carried into, I think, 1979-ish was when the second distribution went out. But the real thing was that we'd kind of hit the limit of what the PDP-11 could do. And DEC had just come out with this new machine called a VAX, which was a 32-bit processor. So it would have, obviously, a much bigger address space. And one of the other research groups at Berkeley actually bought a VAX. In fact, its serial number was 7. It was the seventh one that DEC had built. And so they got it because they were doing a thing called VAXIMA, which was essentially differential equations and other sort of higher-order math. And it was all written in LISP, and LISP, of course, needs, you know, half a megabyte just to get a prompt and, you know, more after that when you start doing anything. And so they just had to have this bigger address space machine. And of course, it came with VMS, which was the DEC operating system, which was kind of a typical operating system of the time, which is to say pretty lame. And so Bill was like, well, we should be running Unix on this machine. Instead of this crappy, you know, vendor operating system. So it turned out that some folks at Bell Labs had also gotten a VAX, and they had done a port of their version 7 of Unix to the VAX. But it was just a really basic port. So it worked just like they did on the PDP-11. It didn't use any of the paging hardware or anything on the VAX. It just allocated physical memory and dropped things into it. And so it couldn't run anything that was bigger than the amount of memory you had on the machine. And that was, I think we had a maximal configuration, which was four megabytes of memory, which took an entire cabinet to hold that much memory. Anyway, that would not have been acceptable for the people that owned the machine, the VAX people, because they needed, you know, eight or 12 megabytes of virtual memory. And, you know, if you couldn't run with more than the amount of physical memory, it wouldn't work for them. So Bill found someone else who was doing, Ozalp Babaoglu, who was doing his PhD thesis on essentially virtual memory, writing a virtual memory system. And so Bill said, well, I'll take your virtual memory system, which was like a PhD prototype and drop it into the Unix that we got, you know, from 32V and we'll bring up, you know,

VM Unix. Well, the only time, and there's only one machine, you have to have a machine to work on to do this. And the only time when it could be done was in the Christmas break. So from about the middle of December to the middle of January, he had four weeks to basically do this. And I happened to be in Berkeley over that period of time because I was trying to get work done and with less people doing stuff, I got more time on the machine. And so I would be sitting there, you know, working away to be running the, you know, the VMS system. And then a message would come up, you know, shutting down to reboot VM Unix, you know, and so quickly, you know, write everything out and then the VM Unix prompt would come and I'd log back in and I'd be working away, working away, and then suddenly everything would freeze. And then about a minute later, it would come up with the prompt for VMS again, you know. But the periods of time that it ran, VM Unix got longer and longer as the weeks went by. And finally, by mid-January, when it was do or die, it really wasn't quite working yet, but he's like, oh no, we're going to, you know, we're going to go with it. And it was touch and go for the last two weeks of January because then people actually started trying to use it and the people doing VAXIMA were getting pretty fed up with having the machine crashing all the time. But, you know, Bill persisted and finally by the end of January, it was stable enough that we were committed and they're going forward, we had VM Unix at that point. So now, of course, it comes time to do the third Berkeley distribution, except now instead of just being a bunch of utilities that you're going to drop into an existing system, we're wanting to ship the whole system, the operating system and everything that goes with it. And that included, of course, a whole bunch of AT&T code. And you know, Berkeley had a license to use that, but, you know, you couldn't send it to just anybody, whoever you sent it to also had to have a license. And Bill wasn't all that good about dealing with licenses. I mean, they would call, you know, someone would call up and say, oh, we want it. And he'd say, oh, do you have an AT&T license? Like, oh yeah, we do. It's like, okay, fine. And he'd ship it. Well, some folks at Berkeley and, you know, more on the legal side got a little bit antsy about this. So they ended up hiring somebody whose job it was to actually verify licenses. You know, so somebody wanted it. They, you know, actually got a copy of their license and, you know, checked with AT&T and yes, they're allowed to have it, blah, blah, blah, and then would mail it out. And the mailings have gotten more bigger because there was a whole set of printed manuals that went out and tapes and blah, blah, blah. So at any rate, so they'd start charging $1,000 to just do the license verification and get all the stuff shipped out. And so that then...

became the core of what would ultimately become the Computer Systems Research Group, CSRG. And in particular, the thing that kind of, you know, the next big step that happened was that DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Project Agency,

had all these different contractors, and they were all running different hardware and different operating systems and using different languages. And so somebody would do something, and if they wanted to share it, you know, it was just really difficult because they would be sending it to someone else who would have to port it to whatever they were using and maybe even rewrite it in a different language. And so they said, look, we want to get consistency between our vendors. We want to have, you know, our different research projects. So we want everyone to have the same hardware. We want everyone to run the same operating system. We want everyone to program in the same language. And they fairly quickly decided that the DEC VAX was going to be the hardware because that was, you know, an order of magnitude cheaper than any other 32-bit hardware that was available at the time. And then the next question was, what's the operating system going to be? And, of course, the obvious thing was VMS because that's, you know, what the vendor supports. So, you know, you guide the vendor's hardware, you get their operating system. But there was a faction, including Bill Joy, who said, no, no, no, it shouldn't be that. It should be Unix because Unix is so much better than VMS. And so this big debate went back and forth as to, you know, which operating system it ought to be. And so at some point, a guy named Dave Cashton just said, all right, I'm going to run some benchmarks on the Berkeley Unix and VMS and, you know, see what they show. And he came up with these 10 benchmarks and ran them. And VMS just did better on all of them, some of them substantially better. And so it's like, obviously, we should be using VMS. So Bill gets this report of his and he's looking at it and he would be very animated. He's like, this is the stupidest benchmark. Who cares how fast you can do? Get PID, you know, things like that. He said, but if that's what they're going to decide on, then by golly, we're going to make them run like hell. And so we went through and just super optimized those 10 benchmarks in Berkeley Unix. So we then, you know, we did better than VMS, often by an order of magnitude in some cases, because we kind of cheated. But you do get PID system call once and then you just keep track of it because it wasn't going to change, you know. And so if you did a thousand of them, we do one system call and then we just keep returning the same value after all, you know, without doing any system calls. So, of course, it ran much faster. Anyway, the one place where we couldn't quite get it was the context switching. And. Well, it's an interesting story that I don't really have time to go into, but we are going to. Sorry, go into it.
Well. I actually have a four hour video that goes through all these things, but I don't have four hours right now. Where do I find it?

It's on my website. If you go to www.mckusick.com and there's a history of BSD, just click on that and. That way you'll have this whole thing and in far more detail than I'm doing. Anyway, I wonder sometimes when I hear this thing, I mean, this is right now the period from, let's say, 77 to 82. Bill Joy left at 82, started Sun with his friends, right? Or joined the other people at Sun and was one of the co-founders. How was it at this time? Were already this like companies that now then got really well known, like Microsoft and Apple and the things that we now see very well known? Or were there also like 200 small companies that all built computers and everyone was basically using like.

Other people than not the things that were like 10 years later, the majority of computers. Yeah, well, at that point in time, you're right. IBM had a lock pretty much on the business computers and Microsoft had a lock on the operating system for the other machines. And, you know, as someone said, nobody ever got fired for using IBM. And, you know, so it was viewed that those two just had a complete lock on the market. So and yeah, there were other companies that were trying to do things. And, you know, they mostly were built around particular.

Technology, so CAD cam, for example, there were several companies that did that, and so they had their own computers and operating systems that ran their CAD cam software. And so they had a, you know, a niche market that they would do. When Bill went off to form Sun Microsystems, he was trying to convince me that I should come along and be employee number one or not number one, but a single digit employee. And, you know, I said, you know, Bill, what makes you think that, you know, you're going to suddenly be so successful? I said, we're going to have commodity hardware and commodity software. And, you know, that that's, you know, that's what's going to do it. And I had gotten my master's degree in business administration. And so I explained to him how, you know, all the reasons this wasn't going to work. And so I did ultimately go and consult for them. And so I got a chunk of a small chunk of Sun stock, which ended up being very lucrative in the longer run. But I ended up, you know, Bill left. And so that's when I ended up essentially taking over, you know, well, actually together with a gentleman named Mike Karels of running the CSRG. And we did the later distributions. And eventually got out from underneath the AT&T licensing. I mean, the original AT&T licensing was very inexpensive, but they kept raising the price. And so it eventually got to the point where people were really lobbying to be able to get the software. And so we do another long process that is on that video that I pointed you at. Essentially managed to get rid of all the AT&T code that was in BSD so that we were able to freely redistribute it. That resulted in being sued by AT&T. But they ultimately lost that lawsuit because, in fact, we had done what we said we had done. And that's how the open source version of BSD came to pass, which is today as FreeBSD, NetBSD and OpenBSD. And at this time, how was the feeling in Berkeley? How did people felt engaged? I mean, I was in Berkeley 10 months ago for a longer period. And it's really nice, but I cannot imagine how it was back in the days. It was probably different. Was it like how a lot of people describe it in the books, like more counterculture and people just being around and building things? Can you describe it a bit?

Well, I mean, there were a bunch of us that were just, you know. It was like this open field, you know, you could there were just all these things that just made sense to do, you know, and people just did it. And the fact that it ultimately became so important was was secondary. I mean, that that wasn't our goal. We were just enjoying doing the things we were doing. And, you know, I mean, what's the secret to success? Well, be in the right place at the right time. I mean, with the Internet, you know, we thought, oh, you know, we're making all this information that used to only be available to the elite suddenly available to the common man. This can be nothing but good. We had no idea that it would be weaponized to the way it has been today. I mean, it's just like it didn't even occur to us that that could happen. I mean, looking back in retrospect, of course, that's what's going to happen. I mean, that's what inevitably seems to happen. But, you know, ideally, we just figured, you know, nothing but good could come of it.

So then after Bill left, you and what is the name again of the other guy you took together over the BSD? After Bill left, you you basically. Oh, yeah. So after Bill left, rather than going with him to Sun Microsystems, you know, I had I thought about a year to finish my PhD. And, you know, I was I all too often seen people leave and then, you know, not finish their PhD. And so I really did want to get that done. I want that pin in the in the puzzle. And so I figured, you know, it'll take me a year to do that. By then, it'll be obvious whether Sun is going to actually, you know, be successful or not. And if they are, then I can go off and join them. Well, of course, it took me a year to do that. And so I figured, you know, it'll take me a year to do that.

It took me a couple more years to finish my PhD. And by the time I had done that, Sun was off and running and was 1,000 employees, et cetera. Although, one of the things that Sun wanted was the Pascal compiler. And so I got hired as their very first consultant. In fact, it's just handwritten on a piece of paper that's signed by Bill and Vinod, then CEO, with my contract. And I actually learned something very valuable. That was one of my first consulting contract. And the thing is that startups, they're short on cash, but they got lots of stock. And in those days, the rules about stock was a lot looser and goosier than it is today. So I would say, all right, I have this super high consulting rate, or what seemed like a super high consulting rate. But you can pay half of it to me in stock and half in cash. And they universally went for that for reasons they could go into. But when I left the university, I decided that which company would I go to. But while I was making up my mind, I would just continue consulting. And to this day, I'm still consulting. I never actually went to a company. But over my career, I've worked with about 30 different companies that I've gotten stock in. And of those, 26 are wallpaper. Three of them have actually cashed out. And one, not clear what's going to happen yet. And I only had a few thousand shares of stock. But in each case, cashed out for $1 to $2 million. And so by the time I was 40, I had enough money that I could theoretically retire. I sort of tried to do that, but I was bored out of my skull. So I gave up on that plan. And in fact, even today, now that I'm in my 70s, I'm still doing a bit of consulting. But instead of having this retirement cliff, I've just been kind of winding down. So I only have about maybe 25% time I'm working now. And the projects I am doing are all things that I would do anyway. So might as well get paid to do them, open source software. And so that's working out for me. When you consulted these early stage startups, what did you try to find out to help them then in the right way? Or what was something you saw as a thing that often went wrong where you then gave good advice?

So a lot of what I did is piecemeal stuff. So early on, there were a bunch of companies that knew they needed to do something with the internet, but they didn't really understand what the internet was and how to do it. And so I would go in and help them design their products, do design reviews. I have a class I teach. And I would go in and teach them the piece of the class that was specific to what the product was that they were trying to build. And so the sorts of errors that were just chronically being made was not understanding what the technology was capable of, but also not understanding what it was not capable of doing. And so they would be doing these things where they, in a day when you might get a megabit of bandwidth, and they were going to need a gigabit of bandwidth for what their product was going to do. And it's like, no, that's just not going to work. And this is why. And you need to rethink the way that you're doing stuff here so that you can work within the constraints of what's available to you. So those were the sorts of problems that they were having. Other ones were they were starting to use C++. And C++ is a kitchen sink. You can simply not use all of the features of it because there's stuff that overlaps and doesn't interact well together. And so if you're going to use C++, the first thing you need to do is subset the language and say, all right, we're going to use this set of features, and we are specifically not going to use this other set of features. And of course, what you need to pick is somewhat dependent on the product you're building. But right from the get-go, just saying, all right, you're going to use C++. Let's figure out what part of C++ we're going to use. And the number of companies that I saved from going down that rat hole was large. And did you also, I don't know, what were the most interesting company you helped with? Did you help some of the big companies that we know today?

Well, Sun, of course, they're not here anymore. Network Appliance, Juniper Networks, oh, come on. Another one of the networking companies down in the South Bay. Even Cisco, a little bit, I did a little bit of work with them, although they kind of didn't follow my advice and went off the rails. But on that particular product. What do you think when you saw people trying to build products that then use new technologies and use maybe the internet, what does it take or what is the most important steps and process you have to start with to build a really great product with the range of a new technology?

Well, I mean, the goal is to come up with a product that's going to be a useful product. And that's where the entrepreneur idea has to come in. So Network Appliance built this sort of the first of the storage systems that was just on the net. And historically, your disks are directly connected to a very high speed backplane bus to your processor. And here they wanted to build one that was the disk was going to be on the other end of a network connection. And so they really have to do some optimizations to make that work effectively, because you don't have the bandwidth you would have for a directly connected disk. The flip side is that you can have a whole bunch of different computers that are all accessing that disk at the same time. And so that was the inspiration. And that, of course, has proven to be a very workable design, especially as networks have gotten faster. So I mean, they were kind of depending on the fact that networks had to get faster, but they have. And so that was sort of the key idea there. Juniper Networking was this concept that historically the routers were custom built hardware. And the idea that they came up with was we can just use a general purpose computer running a general purpose operating system with a little bit of specialized hardware, and we can build a router that is scalable. And we'll be able to run at the kind of speeds that people need. And the companies that were building the custom hardware like Cisco, they had to keep rebuilding as new generations of hardware became available. Whereas Juniper, they just bought off the shelf commodity hardware and let the hardware people do all of the hardware design. All they did was software that they could just keep dropping on faster and faster hardware with just a little bit of their own added hardware. And I mean, Cisco eventually realized that Juniper had a good idea and started doing that. But that was kind of the key idea there. And that was revolutionary for its time. And it continues to be the right way to do things. And I mean, everyone recognizes that and does it that way today.

From this early consulting time, do you have any strange story in mind that's happened or any story that you can remember that shaped you? I mean, there's interesting stories, but there's sort of more personal people stories. And I don't really want to put them out there without the consent of those people.
OK. So after then, the first time when you talked to the people who were building the hardware, what was the first thing that came to your mind?

Together with the BSD and the Berkeley, how fast was it then that you changed BSD to free BSD? And what were the transitions there? Like you said, the license thing, you brought down a bit. And you started then directly changing it to a free version. And then what happened after that? Well, the sort of steps were we started working on getting a freely redistributable version of the networking. That was the first thing. So in the mid-80s, maybe 85-ish, they had their PCs, which were running Microsoft. But the PC.

BSD itself was just not capable of doing networking. It just didn't have enough processing power, address space, et cetera. And so the way you would get networking was you would buy a separate networking card that you would plug in that would interact just through the regular PC backplane. But that card had a processor on it, so all of the TCP processing was being done on that card, and then just sort of the connection information was being, you know, the remote login or the remote copy or whatever it was, was the only part that went back and forth to the PC itself.
